title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
author: Frederick Douglass
era: 1845 (Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave)
openingText: I was born in Tuckahoe, near Hillsborough, about twelve miles from Easton, in Talbot County, Maryland. I have no reliable knowledge of my own age, since I have never seen any official record of it. Most slaves know as little about their ages as horses do about theirs, and nearly every master I knew of wanted to keep them that ignorant. I cannot remember ever meeting a slave who could name his birthday.
about:
Frederick Douglass wrote this short book in 1845, about seven years after he escaped from slavery in Maryland and at roughly the age of twenty-seven. He wrote it partly to answer a charge: audiences who heard him speak on the abolitionist circuit could not believe that so capable a man had ever been a slave, and some doubted he had been one at all. His reply was to set down the facts — the county he was born in, the names of the men who owned and beat him, the plantations, the dates he could reconstruct — knowing that he was still legally a fugitive and that publishing them put his own freedom at risk.

The Narrative follows his life from a Maryland plantation to the city of Baltimore, where a mistress began teaching him to read until her husband forbade it; through the brutal months with the slave-breaker Edward Covey and the fight that broke Covey's hold on him; to a failed escape, a return to the Baltimore shipyards, and at last the successful flight north in 1838. Running through it is a single argument made in the open: that slavery degrades the people who own slaves as surely as those they hold, and that learning to read was, in Douglass's own words, the pathway from slavery to freedom. A closing Appendix draws a hard line between the Christianity of Christ and the slaveholding religion that blessed the whip. It became the most widely read of the American slave narratives and the foundation of Douglass's life as a writer and statesman.

angleCards.title: Literacy as the pathway out of slavery.
angleCards.text: In Baltimore, Sophia Auld begins teaching the boy his letters, until her husband stops her with the warning that learning would forever unfit him to be a slave. Douglass takes the warning as a revelation and sets out to learn by any means — trading bread to poor white boys for lessons, copying letters off ship-timber, writing in the gaps of a copy-book. Watch how reading first frees him and then torments him, opening his eyes to a condition he cannot yet escape.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the literacy thread — Mr. Auld's warning, the Columbian Orator, and the tricks Douglass used to learn to read and write — and how knowledge both freed and tormented him.

angleCards.title: How slavery corrupts the master.
angleCards.text: Douglass insists that slavery deforms the people who hold power as much as those who suffer under it. His clearest proof is Sophia Auld, who meets him as a kind, tender-hearted woman and is slowly turned by the habit of ownership into someone who snatches a newspaper from his hands in fury. Trace the change in her, and in Thomas Auld after his conversion, as the system does its work on them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to watch Douglass's argument that slavery corrupts the slaveholder — especially the change in Sophia Auld from kindness to cruelty — as it plays out across the book.

angleCards.title: The fight with Covey.
angleCards.text: Sent to the slave-breaker Edward Covey, Douglass is worked and whipped until he is nearly broken in body and spirit. The chapter turns on a single morning when he decides to fight back and grapples with Covey for two hours. He calls it the turning point in his life as a slave — the moment he recovers the sense of himself as a man. Read it as the hinge of the whole book.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Covey chapter closely — the breaking, the two-hour fight, and why Douglass calls it the turning point in his life as a slave.

angleCards.title: The Christianity of Christ against the slaveholding religion.
angleCards.text: Douglass attacks religion throughout the book, then uses the Appendix to draw a line he does not want misread: his target is the slaveholding religion of America, not Christianity itself. He sets the pious master who whips on Monday and preaches on Sunday against the Christianity of Christ. Read the Appendix to see how carefully, and how furiously, he keeps the two apart.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Appendix on religion — the distinction Douglass draws between the Christianity of Christ and the slaveholding religion of this land.

cast.name: Frederick Douglass
cast.description: The author telling his own life from the inside, born into slavery in Maryland around 1818 and writing here as a free man of about twenty-seven. He withholds nothing he can safely prove, naming the people and places that made him. His voice is controlled, exact, and morally relentless.

cast.name: Sophia Auld
cast.description: Douglass's Baltimore mistress, who had never owned a slave before him and at first treats him as a fellow human being, even beginning to teach him to read. Under the influence of slaveholding, her kindness curdles into cruelty. Douglass offers her as his clearest evidence that the system poisons the people who hold power within it.

cast.name: Hugh Auld
cast.description: The Baltimore master in whose household Douglass spends much of his youth, and the man who forbids his wife to teach the boy to read. His warning that literacy would ruin a slave hands Douglass the very idea that drives him toward freedom. He later pockets the wages Douglass earns in the shipyards.

cast.name: Edward Covey
cast.description: A poor, church-going farmer hired to break rebellious slaves through relentless labor and surprise beatings. He nearly succeeds with Douglass before losing a two-hour fight that he never reports, to protect his reputation. The struggle against him is the turning point of the book.

cast.name: Thomas Auld
cast.description: Douglass's legal owner for part of the narrative, a mean and insecure man who came into his slaves by marriage. After a camp-meeting conversion he grows crueler rather than kinder, finding religious sanction for the lash. He stands at the center of Douglass's case against slaveholding piety.

cast.name: The Pathway from Slavery to Freedom
cast.description: Douglass's own name for literacy — the reading and writing that a master tries to deny him precisely because it is so dangerous. It does not free his body, but it remakes his mind, and it is what finally lets him imagine and reach the North. The idea organizes the whole second half of the book.

acclaim.quote: This Narrative contains many affecting incidents, many passages of great eloquence and power.
acclaim.context: Preface to the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845

acclaim.quote: Every one who has heard you speak has felt, and, I am confident, every one who reads your book will feel, persuaded that you give them a fair specimen of the whole truth.
acclaim.context: Letter printed in the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845

acclaim.quote: Considered merely as a narrative, we have never read one more simple, true, coherent, and warm with genuine feeling.
acclaim.context: review in the New-York Daily Tribune, 10 June 1845

whyItMatters.title: A first-hand witness who names names
whyItMatters.body: Douglass wrote the Narrative to be believed. Abolitionist audiences doubted that so articulate a speaker could really have come out of slavery, so he answered with specifics no invented story would risk: the county of his birth, the names of the men who owned and whipped him, the plantations, and the dates he could reconstruct. He did this while still legally a fugitive, knowing the book could be used to recapture him. The result is testimony rather than memoir at a safe distance — one of the few accounts of American slavery written by a person who had lived inside it and could prove it. It remains a primary source historians still rely on to know what bondage looked like from below.

whyItMatters.title: Reading as the road out of bondage
whyItMatters.body: The book's central drama is not an escape but an education. When Hugh Auld forbids his wife to teach the boy his letters — because learning would make him unfit to be a slave — Douglass realizes that literacy is exactly what his masters fear, and sets out to get it by any means he can. He trades bread to poor white children for lessons and practices writing on fences and in the margins of a copy-book. Reading then turns on him, showing him the full horror of his condition before it can offer any way out. Every later argument about who is allowed to learn, and why, runs back through this account of a child stealing an education.

whyItMatters.title: The Christianity of Christ and the slaveholding religion
whyItMatters.body: Douglass spends the book exposing masters who pray and whip in the same week, then devotes the Appendix to making sure the attack is not mistaken for an attack on faith itself. He separates the Christianity of Christ from what he calls the slaveholding religion of America — the piety that blesses the auction block and funds the pulpit with blood-stained gold. The distinction is drawn with deliberate care and real fury, and it is one of the sharpest pieces of religious criticism written in the nineteenth century. It still frames the question of how a religion can be claimed on both sides of the same injustice.
